citations.text: ochrane Library, ScienceDirect, Scopus, and LILACS databases. Of the 535 studies initially identified, five randomized controlled trials met the eligibility criteria, totaling 187 participants, predominantly sedentary adults and older adults. Three studies investigated individuals with OSA and two involved populations with insomnia. Intervention protocols were mainly based on structured aerobic exercise, particularly walking, performed at least three times per week at moderate to vigorous intensity. The studies reported significant reductions in symptoms of depression, anxiety, and fatigue, as well as improvements in sleep quality and daytime sleepiness. Regular aerobic exercise yields clinically relevant improvements in mental health and sleep outcomes in individuals with OSA and insomnia; however, the evidence remains limited by the low number of randomized trials, heterogeneous protocols, and small sample sizes.

citations.text: Poor sleep quality is common among older adults, affecting health and well-being. Physical activity is a promising nonpharmacological option, but the comparative effects of different exercise types remain unclear. This study compared various physical activity interventions on subjective sleep quality in older adults through network meta-analysis. A systematic search of PubMed, Embase, and Scopus identified eligible evaluating physical activity effects on sleep quality in adults aged ≥60 years. Sleep quality was measured using the Pittsburgh Sleep Quality Index. Interventions were categorized as aerobic, resistance, balance, flexibility, or multicomponent training. Bayesian network meta-analysis estimated mean differences (MDs) with 95% credible intervals (CrI). A total of 39 studies involving 3198 participants met the inclusion criteria. Risk of bias was assessed with ROB-2 and SYRCLE, and an overall level of evidence (strong, moderate, weak, or inconclusive) was assigned based on study quality and consistency of findings. Alpha and beta diversity, as well as bacterial taxa changes, were then reported according to these evidence rankings. Twenty-two studies (9 human, 13 animal) were included, comprising 236 participants and 274 animals with CKD. Dietary fiber supplementation demonstrated limited and inconsistent effects on gut microbiota composition in human studies. metadata.title: The effect of dietary fiber based on fermentability and viscosity on the gut microbiome composition in chronic kidney disease: a systematic review of experimental and clinical trials.

citations.text: Modest increases were observed in a small number of genera, including Verrucomicrobia, Akkermansia, Clostridium by inulin, Oscillospiraceae UCG-002, and Subdoligranulum by resistant starch type 2 in human studies, which were not consistent across animal studies. Beta-glucan showed no significant effects on alpha or beta diversity or microbial composition. In contrast, weak evidence from animal studies suggested that beta-glucan may increase alpha diversity. Isolated dietary fiber interventions were associated with variable changes in gut microbiota composition in CKD, with limited consistency across human and animal studies, and no clear pattern based solely on fermentability or viscosity. Future studies should use standardized sequencing approaches, harmonized taxonomic reporting, and detailed characterization of fiber properties to clarify whether specific fibers reproducibly modulate microbial community structure.This trial was registered at PROSPERO as CRD42023483468.
